body.en: Unit 2 examines exponential and logarithmic functions through the mathematical framework of multiplicative change — modeling phenomena where quantities change by equal proportional ratios over equal intervals. Mastery includes exponential compounding derivations, logarithmic identity proofs, semi-log transformations, and logistic growth dynamics.

label.en: ● Exponential Functions & The Multiplicative Rate Principle

body.en:
A function \(f\) is exponential if for any constant input step \(\Delta x\), the output values change by a constant multiplicative factor:

\[ \frac{f(x + \Delta x)}{f(x)} = b^{\Delta x} \quad (b > 0,\; b \neq 1). \]

The standard algebraic form is \(f(x) = a b^x\), where \(a = f(0) \neq 0\) is the initial value and \(b\) is the base factor:

  • Exponential Growth: When \(b > 1\), \(f\) is strictly increasing and concave up (for \(a > 0\)). The growth rate per unit is \(r = b - 1 > 0\).
  • Exponential Decay: When \(0 < b < 1\), \(f\) is strictly decreasing and concave up (for \(a > 0\)). The decay rate per unit is \(r = 1 - b > 0\).
  • Domain & Range: Domain is \((-\infty, \infty)\); range is \((0, \infty)\) for \(a > 0\). Horizontal asymptote is the line \(y = 0\).

label.en: ● Analytical Derivation of the Continuous Compounding Formula

body.en:
Theorem: An initial investment \(P_0\) compounded \(n\) times per year at an annual nominal rate \(r\) grows after \(t\) years to \(A(t) = P_0\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}\). As compounding frequency becomes instantaneous (\(n \to \infty\)), the accumulated amount converges to the natural continuous model:

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} P_0\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} = P_0 e^{rt}. \]

Rigorous Derivation:

Let \(m = \frac{n}{r}\). As \(n \to \infty\), \(m \to \infty\). Substituting \(n = m r\) into the compounding expression yields:

\[ \lim_{n \to \infty} P_0\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt} = P_0 \lim_{m \to \infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right)^{m r t} = P_0 \left[\lim_{m \to \infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right)^m\right]^{rt}. \]

By the fundamental limit definition of Euler's constant \(e = \lim_{m \to \infty}\left(1 + \frac{1}{m}\right)^m \approx 2.71828\), we obtain:

\[ P_0 \left[e\right]^{rt} = P_0 e^{rt}. \]

Base Equivalence: Any exponential model \(f(t) = a b^t\) can be expressed in continuous base \(e\) by setting \(b = e^k \iff k = \ln(b)\), giving \(f(t) = a e^{kt}\). When \(k > 0\) the model exhibits growth; when \(k < 0\) it exhibits decay.

A biological culture contains 800 organisms and grows by 14% every 3 hours. Write an exponential function \(P(t)\) in standard discrete form with base \(b\), and convert it to an equivalent continuous natural base \(e\) model \(P(t) = P_0 e^{kt}\). Compute the population at \(t = 9\) hours.

Step 1 (Discrete Model): Over \(\Delta t = 3\) hours, the population multiplies by \(1 + 0.14 = 1.14\). The number of 3-hour intervals in \(t\) hours is \(t/3\):

\[ P(t) = 800 (1.14)^{t/3} = 800 \left( (1.14)^{1/3} \right)^t \approx 800 (1.0446)^t. \]

Step 2 (Continuous Base e Conversion): Set \(b = (1.14)^{1/3} = e^k\):

\[ k = \ln\left((1.14)^{1/3}\right) = \frac{1}{3}\ln(1.14) \approx \frac{0.131028}{3} \approx 0.04368. \]\[ P(t) = 800 e^{0.04368 t}. \]

Step 3 (Evaluation at t = 9): At \(t = 9\) hours, exactly 3 tri-hour intervals have passed:

\[ P(9) = 800 (1.14)^{9/3} = 800 (1.14)^3 = 800 (1.481544) = 1,185.24 \approx 1,185\text{ organisms}. \]

label.en: Worked Example D — Algebraic Structure & Vieta's Root Relations

body.en:
Solve the quadratic equation \( x^2 - 10x + 25 = 0 \) and verify the sum and product of its roots.

Step-by-step Solution:
  1. Factor into binomials: \( (x - 5)(x - 5) = 0 \implies x = 5 \text{ or } x = 5 \).
  2. Check Vieta's formulas: sum \( = 5 + 5 = \mathbf{10} \) and product \( = (5)(5) = \mathbf{25} \).

question.en:
Level 1 · Foundations

A sample of a radioactive isotope has an initial mass of 250 mg and decays at a continuous rate of 4.8% per day according to \(M(t) = 250 e^{-0.048 t}\), where \(t\) is measured in days. Determine the exact daily multiplicative decay factor \(b\) in the form \(M(t) = 250 b^t\), and calculate the daily percentage loss rounded to two decimal places.

solution.en:
Multiplicative Base: Rewrite \(e^{-0.048 t} = (e^{-0.048})^t\):

\[ b = e^{-0.048} \approx 0.953134. \]

The exact base is \(b = e^{-0.048}\) (or approximately 0.9531).

Daily Percentage Loss: The percentage decay rate per day is \(1 - b\):

\[ 1 - 0.953134 = 0.046866 \implies 4.69\%. \]

The daily percentage loss is 4.69% (distinguished from the continuous rate of 4.80%).

blocks.heading: Level 2 · Medium — Logarithmic Properties, Inverses & Half-Life / Doubling Time Models

body.en: Prove the fundamental properties of logarithms from exponential identities, compute doubling and half-life intervals analytically, and manipulate transcendental equations.

label.en: ● Logarithmic Functions as Inverses & Property Derivations

body.en:
The logarithm with base \(b > 0, b \neq 1\) is the exact inverse of the exponential function \(f(x) = b^x\):

\[ y = \log_b(x) \iff b^y = x \quad (x > 0). \]

Properties Derived from Index Laws:

  1. Product Identity: \(\log_b(M N) = \log_b M + \log_b N\).
    Proof: Let \(u = \log_b M\) and \(v = \log_b N\). Then \(b^u = M\) and \(b^v = N\). Multiplying gives \(M N = b^u b^v = b^{u+v}\). By definition of logarithm, \(\log_b(M N) = u + v = \log_b M + \log_b N\).
  2. Quotient Identity: \(\log_b\left(\frac{M}{N}\right) = \log_b M - \log_b N\).
    Proof: \(\frac{M}{N} = \frac{b^u}{b^v} = b^{u-v} \implies \log_b(M/N) = u - v = \log_b M - \log_b N\).
  3. Power Identity: \(\log_b(M^k) = k \log_b M\).
    Proof: \(M^k = (b^u)^k = b^{k u} \implies \log_b(M^k) = k u = k \log_b M\).
  4. Change of Base Theorem: \(\log_b(x) = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b} = \frac{\log_c x}{\log_c b}\).
    Proof: Let \(y = \log_b x\). Then \(b^y = x\). Take the natural log of both sides: \(\ln(b^y) = \ln(x) \implies y \ln(b) = \ln(x) \implies y = \frac{\ln x}{\ln b}\).

label.en: ● Analytical Formulas for Doubling Time & Half-Life

body.en:
Doubling Time (\(t_d\)): For an exponential growth model \(P(t) = P_0 e^{rt}\) (with \(r > 0\)), the doubling time is the solution to \(P(t) = 2P_0\):

\[ P_0 e^{r t_d} = 2 P_0 \implies e^{r t_d} = 2 \implies r t_d = \ln(2) \implies t_d = \frac{\ln(2)}{r}. \]

For discrete base \(b\): \(t_d = \frac{\ln(2)}{\ln(b)}\).

Half-Life (\(t_h\)): For an exponential decay model \(A(t) = A_0 e^{-kt}\) (with \(k > 0\)), the half-life is the solution to \(A(t) = \frac{1}{2}A_0\):

\[ A_0 e^{-k t_h} = \frac{1}{2} A_0 \implies e^{-k t_h} = 2^{-1} \implies -k t_h = -\ln(2) \implies t_h = \frac{\ln(2)}{k}. \]

These formulas establish that doubling time and half-life depend strictly on the rate parameter, completely independent of the starting quantity \(P_0\) or \(A_0\).

label.en: ▲ AP Exam Traps & Pitfalls — Exponential & Logarithmic Functions

body.en:
• Domain Verification for Logarithms: In \(\log_b(g(x))\), the argument must be strictly positive: \(g(x) > 0\). Algebraic manipulations can introduce extraneous roots where \(g(x) \le 0\). Always substitute proposed solutions into the original unsimplified equation.
  • Annual Base vs. Continuous Rate: The annual growth factor \(b\) in \(a b^t\) and continuous rate \(r\) in \(a e^{rt}\) satisfy \(b = e^r\). For \(r = 0.05\), \(b = e^{0.05} \approx 1.05127 \neq 1.050\). Confusing discrete with continuous models loses points on FRQs.
  • False Logarithm Distributive Law: Remember that \(\ln(A + B) \neq \ln A + \ln B\)! The log of a sum cannot be expanded. Conversely, \(\ln(A B) = \ln A + \ln B\).
  • Semi-log vs. Log-log Identification: If the plot of \((x, \ln y)\) is linear, the model is exponential (\(y = a b^x\)). If the plot of \((\ln x, \ln y)\) is linear, the model is a power function (\(y = a x^k\)).

A sample of Carbon-14 has a known half-life of 5,730 years. An archaeological artifact currently contains 38% of its original Carbon-14 concentration. Formulate the exponential decay model \(A(t) = A_0 e^{-kt}\), find the exact decay constant \(k\), and determine the age of the artifact to the nearest decade.

Step 1 (Find Decay Constant k):

\[ A(t) = A_0 e^{-kt} \implies \frac{1}{2} A_0 = A_0 e^{-k(5730)} \implies e^{-5730 k} = \frac{1}{2}. \]\[ -5730 k = \ln(0.5) = -\ln(2) \implies k = \frac{\ln(2)}{5730} \approx 1.20968 \times 10^{-4}. \]

Step 2 (Set Up Age Equation): The remaining fraction is \(A(t)/A_0 = 0.38\):

\[ e^{-kt} = 0.38 \implies -kt = \ln(0.38) \implies t = -\frac{\ln(0.38)}{k} = -\frac{\ln(0.38)}{\frac{\ln(2)}{5730}} = 5730 \cdot \frac{\ln(1/0.38)}{\ln(2)}. \]

Step 3 (Evaluation):

\[ t = 5730 \cdot \frac{-\ln(0.38)}{\ln(2)} \approx 5730 \cdot \frac{0.967584}{0.693147} \approx 5730 \cdot 1.39593 \approx 7,998.7\text{ years}. \]

Rounding to the nearest decade, the artifact is approximately 8,000 years old.

question.en:
Level 2 · Medium

Solve the logarithmic equation \(\log_2(x + 3) + \log_2(x - 1) = 5\) analytically for all real solutions. Show the verification step that eliminates extraneous roots.

solution.en:
Step 1 (Apply Product Property):

\[ \log_2((x + 3)(x - 1)) = 5. \]

Step 2 (Convert to Exponential Form):

\[ (x + 3)(x - 1) = 2^5 = 32. \]

Step 3 (Solve the Quadratic Equation):

\[ x^2 + 2x - 3 = 32 \implies x^2 + 2x - 35 = 0. \]\[ (x + 7)(x - 5) = 0 \implies x = -7 \quad \text{or} \quad x = 5. \]

Step 4 (Domain Verification):

For \(x = -7\): \(x - 1 = -8 \le 0\), and \(\log_2(-8)\) is undefined in the real numbers. Hence \(x = -7\) is an extraneous solution.

For \(x = 5\): \(5 + 3 = 8 > 0\) and \(5 - 1 = 4 > 0\). Checking: \(\log_2(8) + \log_2(4) = 3 + 2 = 5\). Valid!

The unique real solution is \(x = 5\).

blocks.heading: Level 3 · Advanced — Semi-Log Transformations & Logistic Population Modeling

body.en: Linearize non-linear empirical datasets through logarithmic transformations and analyze bounded carrying-capacity dynamics in logistic models.

1. Semi-Log Model (Exponential):

Suppose the transformation \(Y = \ln(y)\) plotted against \(x\) forms a straight line with slope \(m\) and vertical intercept \(c\):

\[ \ln(y) = m x + c. \]

Exponentiating both sides base \(e\):

\[ y = e^{m x + c} = e^c \cdot e^{m x} = e^c \cdot (e^m)^x = a b^x, \]

where \(a = e^c\) and \(b = e^m\). Thus, linearity on a semi-log plot proves that \(y\) is an exponential function of \(x\).

2. Log-Log Model (Power Function):

Suppose the transformation \(Y = \ln(y)\) plotted against \(X = \ln(x)\) forms a straight line with slope \(m\) and vertical intercept \(c\):

\[ \ln(y) = m \ln(x) + c. \]

Exponentiating both sides:

\[ y = e^{m \ln(x) + c} = e^c \cdot e^{\ln(x^m)} = e^c \cdot x^m = a x^m, \]

where \(a = e^c\). Thus, linearity on a log-log plot proves that \(y\) is a power function of \(x\).

label.en: ● The Logistic Growth Model & Asymptotic Carrying Capacity

body.en:
When exponential growth is constrained by environmental or resource limits, populations follow a logistic model:

\[ P(t) = \frac{L}{1 + C e^{-k t}} \quad (L > 0,\; C > 0,\; k > 0), \]

where:

  • Carrying Capacity (\(L\)): \(\lim_{t \to \infty} P(t) = \frac{L}{1 + 0} = L\). The horizontal line \(y = L\) is an upper horizontal asymptote.
  • Initial Population: \(P(0) = \frac{L}{1 + C}\).
  • Point of Maximum Growth Rate: The population grows fastest at exactly half the carrying capacity, \(P = \frac{L}{2}\), which occurs at time \(t = \frac{\ln C}{k}\). At this point, the concavity of the graph transitions from concave up to concave down (inflection point).

A wildlife reserve introduces a herd of elk modeled by the logistic function:

\[ P(t) = \frac{1,200}{1 + 19 e^{-0.18 t}}, \]

where \(t\) is measured in years since introduction. (a) State the carrying capacity and initial herd size. (b) Find the herd population when it is growing at its maximum rate, and calculate the exact year when this occurs. (c) Determine when the herd reaches 90% of its carrying capacity.

Part (a): Carrying capacity is the numerator: \(L = \mathbf{1,200}\text{ elk}\). Initial herd size at \(t = 0\): \[ P(0) = \frac{1200}{1 + 19 e^0} = \frac{1200}{20} = \mathbf{60}\text{ elk}. \]

Part (b): Maximum growth rate occurs at half the carrying capacity: \[ P = \frac{1200}{2} = \mathbf{600}\text{ elk}. \] Set \(P(t) = 600\): \[ \frac{1200}{1 + 19 e^{-0.18 t}} = 600 \implies 1 + 19 e^{-0.18 t} = 2 \implies 19 e^{-0.18 t} = 1. \]\[ e^{-0.18 t} = \frac{1}{19} \implies -0.18 t = -\ln(19) \implies t = \frac{\ln(19)}{0.18} \approx \frac{2.9444}{0.18} \approx \mathbf{16.358}\text{ years}. \]

Part (c): 90% of carrying capacity is \(0.90 \times 1200 = 1,080\) elk:

\[ \frac{1200}{1 + 19 e^{-0.18 t}} = 1080 \implies 1 + 19 e^{-0.18 t} = \frac{1200}{1080} = \frac{10}{9}. \]\[ 19 e^{-0.18 t} = \frac{1}{9} \implies e^{-0.18 t} = \frac{1}{171}. \]\[ -0.18 t = -\ln(171) \implies t = \frac{\ln(171)}{0.18} \approx \frac{5.14166}{0.18} \approx \mathbf{28.565}\text{ years}. \]

question.en:
Level 3 · Advanced

Experimental laboratory data pairs \((x, y)\) are transformed by computing \(Y = \ln(y)\). A linear regression performed on \((x, Y)\) yields the best-fit line \(Y = -0.42 x + 2.85\). Write the corresponding non-linear model for \(y\) as an exponential function of \(x\) in the form \(y = a b^x\), giving \(a\) and \(b\) to three decimal places. Then predict the value of \(y\) when \(x = 5\).

solution.en:
Step 1 (Exponentiate the Linear Equation):

\[ \ln(y) = -0.42 x + 2.85 \implies y = e^{-0.42 x + 2.85} = e^{2.85} \cdot e^{-0.42 x} = e^{2.85} \cdot (e^{-0.42})^x. \]

Step 2 (Compute Parameters):

\[ a = e^{2.85} \approx 17.28775 \approx 17.288, \]\[ b = e^{-0.42} \approx 0.65705 \approx 0.657. \]

The exponential model is \(y = 17.288(0.657)^x\) (or \(y = 17.288 e^{-0.42 x}\)).

Step 3 (Predict for x = 5):

\[ y(5) = 17.288 \cdot e^{-0.42 \times 5} = 17.288 \cdot e^{-2.1} \approx 17.288 \cdot 0.122456 \approx \mathbf{2.117}. \]

question.en: [Unit 2 · Exponential and Logarithmic Functions · Practice 4] If the governing relation for this system is \( g(t) = 6t + 6 \), evaluate \( g(10) \) and find the inverse input \( t \) when \( g(t) = 72 \).

solution.en: Substitute \( t = 10 \): \( g(10) = 6(10) + 6 = \mathbf{66} \). Setting \( 6t + 6 = 72 \) gives \( 6t = 66 \implies t = \mathbf{11} \).
